edges.description: Persistent bacteria aggregate into the non-filamentous grains that define botryomycosis.
Inadequate clearance permits bacteria to persist long enough to organize as compact grains.
Persistent grains sit at the center of a chronic suppurative and granulomatous host reaction.
Chronic dermal inflammation forms nodular cutaneous lesions.
Suppurative inflammation forms abscesses and draining sinuses.
Chronic destructive inflammation can ulcerate the skin surface.
Suppurative inflammation drains to the surface through sinus tracts and fistulae.
In the lung, the pyogranulomatous reaction forms a mass-like lesion.
HIV-associated defects in cellular immunity leave the host less able to clear ordinary pyogenic bacteria.

Local injury or surgery is the usual setting in which bacteria enter and persist in tissue.

evidence.snippet: Patients with botryomycosis typically present multiple nodules, sinuses, abscesses, fistulae, and ulcers, which develop during weeks or months.

nodes.description: In people with HIV and poor immunological control, effective antiretroviral therapy restores the host context; in a reported facial case, repeated antibiotic courses gave only partial and temporary remission, and complete remission followed a darunavir and raltegravir regimen.

evidence.reference_title: Facial botryomycosis-like pyoderma in an HIV-infected patient: remission after initiation of darunavir and raltegravir.
evidence.snippet: Several courses of antimicrobial therapy provided only partial and temporary remission. Complete clinical remission was only achieved 5 years later when a novel antiretroviral regimen composed of darunavir and raltegravir was initiated.

nodes.description: Cocci or bacilli cluster into lobulated, non-filamentous granules at the center of lesions and are frequently coated by eosinophilic Splendore-Hoeppli material.

evidence.reference_title: Botryomycosis: A Case Series and Literature Review in Mexico.
evidence.snippet: The grains, approximately 1 mm in size, are amphophilic, lobulated, and non-filamentous, consisting of coccoid or bacillary elements arranged in clusters, and are located at the center of the inflammatory reaction.

evidence.reference_title: Case of cutaneous botryomycosis in an 8-year-old immunocompetent boy with a review of the published work.
evidence.snippet: Histopathology showed sulfur granules surrounded by an eosinophilic matrix, indicating the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon.

nodes.description: Neutrophils, macrophage-lineage histiocytes, eosinophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibroblasts, and occasional giant cells accumulate around the grains, generating chronic abscessing and granulomatous dermal or visceral lesions.

evidence.reference_title: Botryomycosis: A Case Series and Literature Review in Mexico.
evidence.snippet: Granulomas composed of neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, fibroblasts, histiocytes, and occasionally foreign body-type giant cells are identified in the dermis.

nodes.description: Ordinary non-filamentous pyogenic bacteria enter or persist in damaged tissue rather than being cleared as an acute abscess.

evidence.reference_title: Botryomycosis: A Case Series and Literature Review in Mexico.
evidence.snippet: Botryomycosis is a chronic, suppurative, and granulomatous bacterial infection caused by non-filamentous Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria that are aerobic or microaerophilic and form grains (biofilm composed of masses of bacteria agglomerated by interstitial cement).

nodes.description: Antibacterial therapy is selected from the cultured organism and its susceptibility pattern and typically continues for weeks to months.

evidence.reference_title: Botryomycosis: A Case Series and Literature Review in Mexico.

evidence.reference_title: Botryomycosis: A Case Series and Literature Review in Mexico.
evidence.snippet: The most frequently used regimen was trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, followed by dicloxacillin, resulting in complete resolution of the lesions without evidence of recurrence during follow-up.

nodes.description: Botryomycosis usually follows a skin lesion or surgical intervention, which gives ordinary skin bacteria access to damaged tissue.
